title: Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction to isopropanol using novel carbonized copper metal organic framework derived electrodes
abstract: It is well known in sustainable energy research that metallic copper functions as an electrocatalyst for the reduction of CO2 to multicarbon products such as alcohols and hydrocarbons. However, it remains a great challenge to develop a cost-effective, selective, and stable catalyst/electrode material for this reaction. This work furthers previous studies concerning the potential of carbonized copper MOF-derived electrocatalysts as catalyst materials for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Two commercial copper-decorated metal organic frameworks (MOFs), HKUST-1 and PCN-62, pyrolyzed at variable temperatures, 400−800 °C, were coated on both metallic nickel and copper supports as inks. The electrocatalysts’ potential to reduce CO2 was gauged using an electrochemical cell with both GC-TCD and GC-FID analyses. Many of the previously reported products of this reaction were formed, however, most notably, GC-FID analysis confirmed the formation of isopropanol, a product not previously reported to the best of our knowledge. It was observed that MOF-derived coatings can produce electrodes with both better current density and selectivity towards isopropanol compared to that of uncoated copper electrodes. Amongst all the carbon products observed, the best performing electrocatalyst demonstrated isopropanol faradaic efficiency (FE) of over 72 %. Preliminary techno-economic analysis was conducted to identify target cell operating voltage in order to make the proposed electrochemical CO2 reduction process economically feasible. The desired cell operating voltage is less than 1.9 V, preferably less than 1.6 V. Future work will focus on electrochemical cell design and electrocatalyst morphology to further improve isopropanol selectivity and minimize hydrogen FE.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The increasing industrial emissions of greenhouse gases are having a dramatic effect on global warming and climate change. Carbon dioxide, the main contributor to the greenhouse gas effect, is mainly produced from electricity generation and large manufacturing facilities, equating to 40 % and 20 % of global emissions, respectively [1]. Research, and the implementation therein, of cost-effective carbon capture and sequestration (CSS) technologies in large industrial settings has become an attractive solution to this problem.
From 1850 to 1975, human activities have increased the amount of atmospheric CO2 from 290 ppm to more than 330 ppm [2], and as of 2018, more than 407 ppm [3]. This increase raises concerns that human activities are directly perturbing the CO2 greenhouse equilibrium. With increasing atmospheric concentrations of CO2 augmenting climate change, it is imperative for advancements in technology for carbon capture and utilization. While large-scale CO2 capture methods are
implemented, such as amine-based solvent CO2 capture from flue gas streams with subsequent amine regeneration [4], utilization techniques have yet to achieve full-scale commercialization. Electrocatalytic reduction is an environmentally sustainable option to close the loop between CO2 capture and utilization, with the potential to generate valuable and marketable products [5]. The recycling of CO2 by electrochemical reduction is achieved by supplying electrical energy to maintain a potential between two electrodes in order to convert CO2 into reduced forms [6]. By coupling renewable energy sources, such as wind or solar, the electrocatalytic reduction could yield carbon-negative fuels or industrial chemicals that are conventionally derived from petroleum [7].
Short-chain alcohols such as methanol, ethanol, and propanol are high-value products that may result from the CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction. In 2016 the global market size for industrial alcohols was valued at USD $105.89 billion [8]. The practice of using an ethanol-gasoline blend for fuel is the driving force along with the use of

methanol, isobutanol, and isopropanol for personal care and pharmaceutical applications. Isobutanol and isopropanols’ amphipathic nature also makes these compounds great cleaning solvents for various industries. The global isopropanol market was USD $2.84 billion in 2012 and is projected to reach $4.23 billion by 2018 [9]. To the best of our knowledge, no previous literatures report the formation of isopropanol from this reduction reaction.
Although the idea of energy-dense fuel generation from CO2 is attractive, several limitations have prevented the electrochemical process from achieving larger-scale adaptation: high overpotentials, non-discrete product selectivity, and low faradaic efficiencies. In the electrochemical reduction of CO2, the electrical energy supplied is consumed by several reactions. (1) Water splitting where H2 and O2 are generated, and (2) The reduction of CO2 into various gaseous and liquid products. Due to the thermodynamic uphill barrier, an external bias is required to drive the overall reaction. To drive the one electron transfer of CO2 to CO2•−, the potential required is -1.9 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (SHE), which makes the reaction highly energetic and unfavorable [10]. At the same time, the proton-assisted reactions are more favorable with an electromotive force ranging from -0.2 to 0.2 V (vs. SHE) shown in Table 1. Due to the similarity of redox potentials for these reduction reactions, the electrochemical process leads to a wide range of CO2-derived products. In addition, the utilized electrolyte directly influences the major products formed: alcohols and ethane are favored in solutions of KCl, K2SO4, KClO4, and diluted HCO3- solutions, while methane is preferred from concentrated HCO3- and phosphate solutions [11]. To achieve high selectivities and production rates for a specific product, it is necessary to utilize a selective electrode material that favors the reaction of choice whilst mitigating H2 evolution and other undesirable side reactions.
Transition metals and derivatives have the electrocatalytic ability to reduce CO2 into higher carbon compounds due to the availability of vacant orbitals and active d-electrons that facilitate bonding between the metal and CO2 for adduct formation and the enhancement of converted product desorption [12]. Mechanistically, the protonation of adsorbed CO to form CHO; electrodes that bind CO weaker will produce more gaseous CO than those that bind CO strongly [5]. Of the available metal electrocatalysts, copper is the only known material to date with the ability to form large amounts of hydrocarbons [10] from the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Kuhl et. al [10] produced sixteen different CO2 reduction products on metallic copper surfaces, including: methanol, ethanol, ethylene, allyl alcohol, and propanol.
Several classes of copper-based catalysts have been tried and tested for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at the bench scale. Copperbased nanostructures evidenced increased Faradaic efficiencies for product conversion: Copper nanocrystals (perovskite-type), copper nanoclusters, nanostructured copper alloys, nonporous copper films, and copper nanoflower (chrysanthemum-like) were developed and evaluated for the production of hydrocarbons and alcohols [13]. In
addition, Loiudice et al. [14] found a direct relationship between structure and property relations among copper nanocrystals of variable size and their behavior as electrocatalysts in the CO2 reduction. Munir et al. [15] discovered that Cu-Cu2O, Cu-Cu2O-ZnO, and Cu-ZnO electrodes prepared via electrodeposition produced C1, C2, and C3 species; the Cu-ZnO electrode produced the highest Faradaic efficiency of liquid products (methanol, formate, n-propanol, and acetone) at 97.4 %. Another option for a suitable electrocatalyst for this reaction is the use of carbonized copper MOF-derived materials such as HKUST-1 and PCN62.
A MOF is characterized as a porous material formed by bonding between metal ions and organic linkers, both of which lend the MOF its unique chemical properties. MOFs are a relatively new class of materials that have gained increasing attention in many areas of research due to their remarkably high surface area, high porosity, tunable pore sizes, adjustable chemical functionality, and great chemical stability [16]. They are widely used in energy and environmental applications such as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. [17]. Many MOF materials are being utilized in CO2 photoreduction [18] and for electrochemical CO2 reduction [19]. Cyclic voltammetry studies found that copper (I) MOF-derived species were very selective for CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons and higher alcohols [20]. Via pyrolysis at variable temperatures, MOFs can be transformed into thermally robust, conductive materials that serve as excellent electrocatalysts. Zhao et al. utilized carbonized HKUST-1 (900−1100 °C) as an electrode coating to produce alcohol compounds with total faradaic efficiencies of 45.2–71.2 % at -0.1 to -0.7 V versus RHE; in addition, they found that the onset potential for ethanol formation is among the lowest overpotentials observed for the reduction of CO2 to ethanol [21].
The pore structure, specific surface area, particle diameters, and overall metallic content of MOF-derived materials can be controlled by the pyrolysis temperature. The sizes of copper nanocrystals increase with higher pyrolysis temperatures. One difficulty with this approach is to control the conglomeration of large metal atom clusters that form at elevated temperatures; these aggregations can destroy porosity and decrease catalytic efficiency [21]. To overcome this limitation, MOF nanocrystals can be grown within mesoporous carbons, improving the dispersion between resulting metal clusters upon pyrolysis [22]. Here, we report the findings of both commercially synthesized HKUST-1 and PCN-62 carbonized at 400−800 °C for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in a conventional electrolytic cell without membrane separation at constant potential ranging from -2.0 to -2.5 V vs. silver chloride reference electrode. Interestingly, the results evidence isopropanol as a main reaction product, which deviates from most widely reported C3 alcohol formed in this reaction, n-propanol.

sections.heading: 2.1. Electrochemical experiments
sections.text:
The electrochemical set-up with in-situ gaseous analysis and liquid sampling port used in this work is shown in Fig. 1. A five-port electrochemical cell with a water jacket (Pine Instruments, Durham, NC) was used for all experiments. The ports consisted of the following airtight plugs: one 14/20 PTFE stopper, a 14/20 rubber septum, gas sparging/purging line, a silver chloride reference electrode, and the center port, a 24/25 rubber septum with two holes approximately 1 cm apart that the insulated copper wires connected to both the platinum counter and experimental working electrodes were threaded through. The recirculating water temperature was set at 25 °C. A Gamry Reference 3000 Potentiostat (Gamry Instruments, Warminster, PA) was used for all electrochemical measurements.
The cell was filled with 100mL of 0.05M K2CO3 and was purged with CO2 for an hour prior to any voltage application. CO2 was bubbled through continuously at a rate of 25mL/min throughout the duration of the experiment. Chronoamptometry experiments decreased the voltage from -2.0 to -2.5 in increments of -0.1 V/hour. Just before every voltage change, a syringe was inserted through the rubber septum in order to collect a 1mL sample in close proximity to the working electrode for GC-FID analysis.

sections.heading: 2.2. Liquid and gas analysis
sections.text:
The headspace gaseous products of the reaction were analyzed using an INFICON 3000 Micro GC (INFICON, Bad Ragaz, Switzerland) with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and fast cycling time. The micro GC was calibrated for the detection of hydrogen, oxygen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, ethane, and ethylene oxide. The GC-TCD analyses were split into two methods: method 1 (for % gas molecules using MolSieve 5A PLOT, 10m ×0.32mm ID column and PLOT U, 3m ×0.32mm ID pre-column) and method 2 (for ppm gas molecules using PLOT U, 8m ×0.32mm ID column and PLOT Q, 1m ×0.32mm ID pre-column), which alternated injections every minute and a half. The purpose of alternating methods was to detect both product hydrocarbon products and side reaction gases. A Hewlett Packard 6890 GC (Hewlett-Packard, Palo Alto, CA) with a flame ionization detector (FID) was used for analyzing the alcohol content of the collected liquid samples; the instrument was calibrated for the detection of methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol. GC column used was tested for differentiating n-propanol and isopropanol as shown in Supplemental Information. It was found that retention time for isopropanol was 1.8372min, whereas n-propanol was 2.5204min. This work was focused on isopropanol detection and production; therefore, a calibration curve for n-propanol was not developed at this initial stage of development.
The utilized electrochemical set-up schematic is shown in Fig. 1 along with an illustrative diagram of the electrochemical reduction of
CO2. Due to the applied overpotential, the protons electrochemically reduce on the surface of platinum anode and cause hydrogen evolution along with water splitting as shown in Table 1.

sections.heading: 2.3.1. Synthesis of PCN-62
sections.text: PCN-62 MOF were synthesized based on the procedure described in the Literature [23]. It involves the step of making 5,5′,5′'-((benzene1,3,5-tricarbonyl) tris(azanediyl)) triisophthalic acid (H6TPBTM) by dissolving 1,3,5-Benzenetricarbonyltrichloride (1.593 g, 6.0mmol, FW: 265.48) in anhydrous acetonitrile (60mL) and added dropwise to a solution of 5-aminoisophthalic acid (3.81 g, 21mmol, FW: 181.15) in acetonitrile (60mL). 100mL of anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (THF) was then added to the reaction mixture. Nitrogen was refluxed over the resulting mixture for 24 h. After overnight drying under vacuum (< 0.1mmHg), when the reaction mixture was hot, the precipitated white solid was isolated by filtration and then washed with dry THF, acetonitrile, water, and then methanol to obtain 5,5′,5′'-(benzenetricarbonyltris(azanediyl))triisophthalic acid (3.75 g, 89 % yield, FW:699.53). H6TPBTM (15mg) and Cu (NO3)2·6H2O (30mg) were dissolved in 2mL of N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) in a 4mL Pyrex vial, to which 0.2mL of HNO3 were added to prepare PCN-62. The mixture was heated in an 85 °C oven for 12 h to yield 15mg of blue crystals.

sections.heading: 2.3.2. Synthesis of HKUST-1
sections.text: HKUST-1MOF was made by using a novel hydrothermal method based on the reported procedures in the literature [24,25]. Cupric nitrate hemipentahydrate (6.0 g) was dissolved into 250mL deionized water and added with Benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (4.0 g) in a 250mL of solvent consisting of equal parts of ethanol and deionized water. It was then mixed thoroughly to dissolve completely. The resultant solution mixture was transferred into a 250mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave. It was kept at 110 °C for 18 h in oven to yield small crystals. Then the autoclave was cooled down to room temperature naturally and the blue crystals were isolated by filtration. The suspension was washed several times with the mixture of deionized water and ethanol. Then the mixture was dried to get HKUST-1MOF.

sections.heading: 2.4. MOF ink preparation
sections.text: Both HKUST-1 and PCN-62 were synthesized as mentioned procedure in Section 2.3. Approximately 1 g of the selected MOF was placed in a ceramic boat that was pyrolyzed in a ThermoFisher Scientific Lindberg/Blue M Furnace (ThermoFisher, Waltham, MA) at variable temperatures (400−800 °C). Nitrogen gas purged the furnace at a rate of 10mL/min. The carbonized powder product was visualized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in a JEOL JEM-2000FXS/TEM microscope with LaB6 emitter at 200 kV with a 120 μm condenser lens aperture and 80 μm objective lens aperture inserted. Crystallography of this powder was characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD) with a D8 Advance Bruker AXS X-ray diffractometer (Billerica, MA). Roughly 0.2 g of the carbonized powder was placed in a mortar and pestle and was finely grinded into a 20 % v/v Nafion®® in acetone solution. Care was taken to extract the liquid portion of the grinded mix, whilst avoiding the larger solid particles. Commercial metal electrodes such as Nickel and Copper were placed in a binder oven (Cole-Parmer, Vernon Hills, IL) set at 120 °C, and the ink was dropped on the surface until a thorough coating was observed. Thus Ni-PCN-62, Cu-PCN-62 and CuHKUST, Ni-HKUST coated electrodes were prepared at different furnace temperatures. These coated electrodes were visualized and elementally characterized using a FEI Quanta 200 scanning electron microscope (SEM) (FEI Company, Hillsboro, Oregon) in tandem with an Oxford Inca X-sight energy dispersive spectroscopy x-ray detector (EDS) (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, U.K.)

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Both HKUST-1 and PCN-62 were carbonized and used as precursors to coat commercial metal electrodes with respective ink. Fig. 2 illustrates the preparation methodology of the electrodes. Commercially available MOFs were pyrolyzed into a metal/carbon powder, prepared into inks, and drop coated onto commercially available nickel and copper metallic supports. Crystal structure, electrode morphology, and elemental composition of either the pyrolyzed MOF powder or the final prepared electrode were characterized using powder XRD (Fig. 3), SEMEDS (Fig. 4, Fig. 5), and TEM (Fig. 6). Fig. 3 shows the XRD spectra of the HKUST-1 800 °C powder, which revealed peaks at 2θ=36.406 and 43.311, corresponding to Cu2O residue and Cu (111), respectively. Similar results have been obtained for carbonized PCN-62 600 °C. The
intensity counts of XRD evidences minimal Cu2O compared to Cu, confirming the pyrolysis technique. Fig. 4 shows SEM images of a nickel metallic support surface and the nickel metallic support surface coated with prepared HKUST-1 800 °C in. It is evident that Nafion® polymer/ carbon matrix coats the vast majority of the available surface, leaving little, if none, of the original metallic surface available to the reaction interface. The presence of copper in the carbonized matrix is confirmed in elemental SEM-EDS analysis (Fig. 5). Selecting for a small area in a suspected cluster of copper and carbon material revealed a high concentration of copper along with fluorine from the Nafion® binder.
Carbon was emitted from EDS analysis due to its much higher abundance in the matrix. Fig. 6 shows TEM images of the prepared HKUST-1 powder at 800 °C; the catalysts are composed of irregularly spaced copper nanoparticles in a matrix of porous carbon. However, their crystalline structures are different, with the 800 °C in. showing a greater percentage of larger conglomerations of copper-carbon clusters. This polymer matrix is decorated with irregularly spaced copper/carbon clusters from HKUST-1.
Fig. 7 elucidates the potentiostat and GC-TCD data from an experiment employing Cu-HKUST-1 600 °C as the working electrode. As seen in 7A and 7B, the voltage is decreased stepwise from -2.0 V to -2.5 V in -0.1 V increments hourly; subsequently, this increases the amount of current delivered to the working electrode (∼60 to 100mA, 7B). As soon as the overpotential is supplied to the electrode, hydrogen and oxygen are produced via water splitting. Since CO2 was supplied continuously, there is no decrease in concentration, 7C. These side reactions convert CO2 into valuable liquid and gaseous products such as CO, which acts as an intermediate in multi-carbon product formation 7D.
As seen in 8A, the optimization region of isopropanol production for the tested materials is found to be -2.3 V to -2.4 V. Interestingly, commercial copper has its respective lowest Faradaic efficiency for isopropanol formation at -2.4 V (∼10 %) and the highest at -2.0 V (∼25 %). Cu coated with HKUST-1 carbonized at 600 °C is the only tested catalyst that outperforms uncoated copper in FE for isopropanol at -2.3 V and below, achieving a FE of ∼17 % in this range. While all materials made some amount of isopropanol, select materials formed methane, methanol, and CO. Copper foil slightly outperformed copper mesh in FE for methane, seen in 8B, however, copper coated with PCN62 at 400 °C overachieved both electrodes, achieving a max FE of ∼4%
for methane at -2.3 V. Both copper foil and mesh produced no methanol with the utilized cell configuration and applied potentials, however, three of the tested catalysts evidenced a FE of 3–4 % for methanol at -2.3 to -2.5 V(8C). Copper coated with PCN-62 600 °C also showed higher FE for CO, achieving ∼23 % at -2.4 V (8D). Nickel coated with PCN-62 800 °C also achieved decent FE for CO, with ∼17 % at -2.3 V, a slight improvement over copper mesh and foil electrodes for CO FE using this cell configuration and voltage range (Fig. 8).
From Fig. 9 it is clear that the addition of a carbonized MOF coating increases the current density of a commercial electrode at differing voltages. This observation suggests that copper-MOF derived electrode materials used with this cell configuration and voltages will have better catalytic efficiency for CO2 electrochemical reduction compared to that of pure copper metal and may be able to produce reduced CO2 products more cheaply. Tested nickel-support catalysts were able to achieve even higher current densities than that of copper-support electrodes, on average. In addition, there appears to be little correlation between pyrolysis temperature and current density, suggesting that the entirety of the MOF material is carbonized at these temperatures and that crystal conglomeration is negligible at these small electrode sizes of 4 cm2.
Fig. 10 A–D reports the faradaic efficiencies at -2.4 V for each product detected by gas and liquid chromatography for various electrocatalysts and compares with both commercially available and developed catalysts in literature. To maximize the performance of CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) catalysts, higher selectivity for CO2RR products such as higher alcohols over hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) sought after. Thus, we have decided to focus on the selectivity for CO2RR over HER, specifically, the faradaic efficiencies of isopropanol (FEisopropanol) and the selectivity of isopropanol formation over other carbon products (FEisoproanol/FEother). Table 2 summarizes the results of different electrocatalysts studied in this work. Although both copper foil and copper mesh achieve higher FEisopropanol than the tested catalysts, the MOF-derived catalysts contain only a slight fraction of copper
compared to the bulk metal, suggesting that the high surface area of these catalysts is effective in reduction. Cu-PCN-62 600 °C evidenced the highest faradaic efficiency over HER with the major products as methane (10B) and carbon monoxide (Fig. 10C), along with some isopropanol (10A). The selectivity of FEisoproanol/FEother for Cu-HKUST1 600 °C was found to be highest (2.7 %) with a major product as isopropanol (FE of 22.5 %, 10A), followed by Cu-PCN62 600 °C’s selectivity of 2.0 % (FE of 8.2 % for methane Fig. 10C). Thus, Cu-HKUST1 600 °C seems one of the more promising materials amongst the studied electrocatalysts. From Fig. 10A, isopropanol Faradaic efficiencies with the studied materials were ranked in the following order: Cu Mesh > Cu Foil > Cu HKUST-1 600 °C > Ni PCN-62 800 °C=Cu PCN-62 800 °C > Cu PCN-62 600 °C > La1.8Sr0.2CuO4 [5]>Ni HKUST-1 400 °C > Cu electrode [5]>Ni HKUST-1 600 °C.
The current density ranges from 5−20mA/cm2, for both Cu foil and mesh, produce mainly isopropanol and lower carbon products. Comparing Cu PCN-62 600 °C and Ni PCN-62 800 °C, the Cu-based electrode produced much higher CO (∼25 % FE) opposed to methanol (∼4% FE). It was observed that the high current densities exhibited by the Cu and Cu nano materials at higher voltage ranges produced higher faradaic efficiencies for isopropanol than compared to Ni based materials and lower voltage Cu materials. Ren et al. [26] explained the reason for this behavior due to the rise in local pH at catalytic surface, which leads to the formation of ethylene intermediates to promote propanol production (Table 3).
Based on our experimental results and extensive mechanistic studies conducted by Kopar and coworkers [27], possible electrochemical reduction pathways of CO2 to produce methane and alcohols are shown in Fig. 11. The reduction initiates with a proton-electron transfer binding CO2 to the surface as a *CO2H species. A subsequent proton-electron reduction followed by the release of water forms the key intermediate *CO. Formation of C1 products results from the reduction of the *CO intermediate via proton-electron transfer to produce formyl *CHO and hydroxymethylidyne *COH species (Fig. 11, Pathway A). At high
current densities, 60-140mA/cm2 at -2.0 to -2.5 V, displayed with the Ni-HKUST-1 600 °C catalyst, the *CO species are reduced rapidly to yield methane, while lower current densities, 30−60mA/cm2 from -2.0 to -2.5 V, can lead to methanol, as observed for the Ni-PCN-62 800 °C catalyst. The oxidation of methanol to formate may also occur, however, went undetected by our GC method. The formation of C2 products arises from the dimerization of reduced *CO species via an initial electron transfer forming a CeC bond followed by a proton transfer to give a *C2O2H dimer (Fig. 11, Pathway B). The *C2O2H dimer formation is purported to arise from a square arrangement of the *CO species [28]. Rearrangement and reduction of the oxygenated enol *C2H3O species results in ethanol production, which was only observed for the Ni-PCN-62 catalyst.
At low current densities, reductive *CO dimerization occurs to give the enol *C2H3O (Fig. 11, Pathway C). A high surface density of *CO on the catalyst at lower energies may allow for the formation of a new CeC bond from the radical coupling of *C2H3O with a neighboring *CO. Additional proton-electron transfers and release of water can form a C3 enol species that follows the reductive pathway of ethanol to produce isopropanol. The highest selectivity for isopropanol was observed with the Ni-PCN-62 catalyst. Nickel electrodes have been shown to bind CO strongly, which may account for C3 products [29]. The low production
of ethanol from the catalyst screened in Fig. 11 may stem from ethanol being consumed at the electrode to give isopropanol. Recently, MoS2 electrodes were found to produce t-butanol (C4 product) at very low current densities [30]. The C4 product t-butanol could arise similarly through the mechanism proposed in this work.

sections.heading: 4. Techno-economic analysis of the electrochemical CO2 reduction process
4.1. CO2 electrolysis process
sections.text:
A simplified schematic of the proposed electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ER-CO2) process is shown in Fig. 13. At first CO2 is captured and purified from its source such as power plant flue gas, direct air capture, or cement plant. The objective is to concentrate the CO2 to> 95 vol% and remove contaminants (SO2, NOX) and undesired components (O2). The purified CO2 is premixed with recycled CO2 and fed to the alkaline water CO2 reduction electrolyzer along with process water and recycled electrolyte. Off-grid, renewable electrical power is supplied to the electrolyzer to induce simultaneous water splitting and CO2 reduction. Higher alcohols are the preferred reduction products as they present the most favorable economic viability owing to their higher market price.
Isopropanol (IPA) was considered as the primary product, as demonstrated by the experimental results, along with minor quantities of butanol and ethanol. The effluent stream from the cathode is comprised of unconverted CO2 and byproducts (such as H2, CO, CH4, and higher hydrocarbons). The unconverted CO2 is recovered and recycled back to
the electrolyzer. A standard pressure swing adsorption unit is envisioned to achieve this separation. Utilization of the separated byproducts will depend on the specific CO2 generating process the ER-CO2 process is being integrated into and is thus neglected at this stage. Pure oxygen is generated at the anode and is released to the atmosphere in the proposed ER-CO2 process.
Electrolyte solution is continuously removed from the stacked cell to recover the dissolved alcohols and recycle the alkaline electrolyte solution back to the electrolyzer. The recovered alcohols are further purified into separate alcohol product streams. Although a variety of separation processes could be utilized – such as distillation, liquid-liquid extraction, and membrane separation – simple two-step distillation was used to implement electrolyte and water recycle, and alcohols recovery and purification owing to the boiling point difference between water (100 °C) and IPA (82.5 °C) (Fig. 12).

sections.heading: 4.2. Process assumptions
sections.text:
The ER-CO2 process was sized for the production of 200 ton/day of IPA in order to maintain the initial capital investment at less than $100 million and electrical power consumption at about 100–150 MWe. The purified and concentrated CO2 stream can be made available from a variety of sources. This study assumes it is captured from power plant derived flue gas. As per the 26 U.S. Code § 45Q. Credit for carbon oxide
sequestration [31], a tax credit of $35/ton-CO2 will be offered beyond 2024 when using the CO2 for enhanced oil recovery. In order to provide similar economic incentive to the CO2 producer, the cost of CO2 is assumed to be $35/ton-CO2. The delivered CO2 stream is expected to meet typical EOR pipeline qualify specification, especially associated
with O2 (< 10 ppmv) and sulfur compounds (< 100 ppmv) [32]. The purified CO2 will be fed to RTI’s multistack alkaline water electrolyzer employing cathode coated with carbonized MOF electrocatalysts capable of delivering high faradaic efficiency towards higher alcohols, especially IPA, while minimizing production of hydrogen. It is assumed that, upon further development, IPA faradaic efficiency of 90 % will be achieved with a stack energy efficiency of 70 % resulting in a cell voltage requirement of 1.6 V.
The stack installed cost was estimated based on the DOE projections for alkaline water electrolyzers for hydrogen production at a central facility. Since CO2 electrolyzers will need to incorporate gas feed, and electrolyte removal and recycle, stack installed cost was estimated at 330 $/kW which is almost double the stack installed cost for water electrolyzers for hydrogen production [33]. Although the balance of plant (BOP) associated with the electrolyzer operation will be similar to water electrolysis, additional process steps required for gas and liquids separation, purification and recycle almost double the BOP capital cost. The entire BOP installed cost was calculated at 560 $/kW which is 170 % of the stack installed cost and double the cost for hydrogen production by water electrolysis [34]. The total installed capital cost of 532 $/(kg/day-IPA) generated in this study was about 84 % higher compared to the work published by Jouny et al. for n-propanol [31]. A 50 $/MWh electricity price was assumed for the off-grid renewable energy

that will be used for this process [31]. This assumed cost is only 15 % lower than the 59 $/MWh average electricity price charged to industrial customers across the five U.S. gulf coast states in February 2019 [35]. The $1.5/kg IPA selling price used for this analysis was the average FOB price for the year of 2018 as per ICIS’ Americas Chemicals Outlook 2019 [36]. All assumptions considered in the process are summarized in Table 4. Details about techno-economic analysis are given in Supplemental Information.

sections.heading: 4.3. Economic analysis and NPV
sections.text:
The economic viability of the proposed capital expenditure was valuated using net present value (NPV) method. A summary of the financial model assumptions is provided in Table 5. At first, net profit was calculated by subtracting all the variable and fixed operating and maintenance (O&M) costs from the annual revenue generated from selling the products. The net income tax was then calculated by discounting the net profit with the applicable depreciation for that year. Finally, the annual discounted cash flow was calculated by subtracting the income tax from the net profit. Microsoft Excel’s NPV formula was applied for the entire project lifetime (construction period plus plant
operation lifetime) with 10 % rate of return on investment to estimate the NPV cash surplus. A distribution of the annual operating costs is shown in Fig. 13. The largest contributor to the annual operating cost of alcohols production was the cost of electricity consumed by the CO2 electrolyzer (74 % of the total annual operating cost). This is the result of the assumed cell voltage requirement of 1.6 V and an electricity cost of 50 $/MWh. The second largest contributor was the energy requirements of the BOP at 13 % of the total annual operating cost. The cost of feeds (CO2 and water) and the fixed O&M costs contributed 9% and 4% to the total annual operating cost, respectively. Following the NPV estimation philosophy outlined in the previous section the resulting NPV for the base case is $101,054,978, which is ∼105 % of the installed capital cost. These numbers indicate that the proposed ER-CO2 process is financially attractive when performing at the process assumptions detailed in Table 5. Similar attractive NPV value of $82 million has been reported by Jouny et al. for n-propanol [34] (Fig. 13).

sections.heading: 4.4. Sensitivity analysis
sections.text:
Sensitivity analysis was used to identify the system parameters that had the largest impact on the baseline NPV value. Values of select
system parameters were varied between best-case (representative of an ambitious but feasible case), and a worst-case-scenario (representative of a limiting performance case). The actual system parameters varied, and the specific values used to represent the best- and worst-case scenarios is summarized in Table 6. The tornado plot resulting from the sensitivity analysis is shown in Fig. 14. Project NPV was the most sensitive to IPA selling price as it dictates the annual revenue generation. The second and third most important system parameters were electrolyzer cell voltage and price of electricity. Together, these two parameters decide the operating cost associated with the electrolyzer electricity demand which accounted for 74 % of the total operating cost. Of the five parameters used for the sensitivity study, the project NPV was the least sensitive to the installed capital cost. While IPA selling price and price of electricity will be decided by market dynamics and development of low-cost renewable energy technologies, future work in the development of proposed ER-CO2 process must continue to improve the efficiency of the CO2 reduction electrolyzer by lowering the cell voltage requirement and maximizing IPA faradaic efficiency and fulfil the economic viability.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 into valuable and marketable products presents a financially viable emission mitigation strategy. Several copper-based electrocatalysts were tested for efficacy in the CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction. Many of the reported to-date products of this reaction were formed using these materials as electrocatalysts in a simple electrochemical cell configuration. Additionally, isopropanol, a product that has been unreported to date, was also formed. While we attribute the formation of isopropanol to our process configuration and electrochemical cell parameters, it is evident that the prepared MOF-derived coatings on a copper surface have an increased selectivity for isopropanol formation compared to the uncoated copper
surface. In addition, these coated electrodes are able to produce higher current densities making them potential candidates to boost the efficiency of a stacked cell electrolyzer.
Careful engineering and designs are needed for appropriate process design, scale up and integration with cheap renewable energy. Preliminary techno-economic assessment and sensitivity analysis was used to derive process operating conditions that led to an economically feasible electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ER-CO2) process. An end-oflife net present value of over $100 million (105 % of the initial capital investment) is feasible but requires> 90 % faradaic efficiency (FE) towards isopropanol and an electrochemical cell operating at> 70 % energy efficiency. In addition, development of a catalyst that is stable, robust, and cost-effective for this reaction is necessary. While these data suggest promise in the use of MOF-derived electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2, studies concerning electrocatalyst materials and morphology along with an optimized electrochemical cell design are necessary for further evaluation.
